questions.question: Q: Why is iron the endpoint of stellar fusion?

points.text: Fusing iron or heavier elements absorbs energy rather than releasing it, so the star can no longer produce outward pressure to support itself.

questions.question: Q: How are elements heavier than iron produced?

points.text: They are produced during supernova explosions (r-process) and neutron star mergers, where extreme conditions allow rapid neutron capture to build heavier nuclei.

questions.question: Q: What is the triple-alpha process?

points.text: Three helium-4 nuclei (alpha particles) fuse to form carbon-12. This occurs in the cores of red giants after hydrogen fusion ends.

questions.question: Q: Explain the statement 'we are made of star stuff'.

points.text: Most elements in the human body (carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron etc.) were created by nucleosynthesis in stars and dispersed into space by stellar winds and supernovae, later forming the Solar System.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between the proton-proton chain and the CNO cycle?

points.text: Both fuse hydrogen to helium, but the p-p chain is dominant in lower-mass stars (like the Sun) while the CNO cycle uses C, N, O as catalysts and dominates in stars above ~1.3 solar masses.
